try hard not think about the trauma

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a single-patient assault trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because it implies multiple victims or identification with other victims rather than the patient's own assault experience. A more self-referential trigger would be expected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
issues.explanation: 'Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening' sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile's self-directed shame and identity-change appraisals. It implies confidence that another person would have prevented the assault, which conflicts with the patient's own vulnerability/self-blame framing in a way that is hard to integrate clinically.

issues.item: Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma in a 70-year-old male, 'medical procedures' plus 'body shame' implies a strong bodily injury/medical aftermath theme, but the rest of the profile does not support that theme. With only offender cues and intrusive thoughts otherwise present, the medical trigger looks insufficiently anchored and may be mismatched to the rest of the assault profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body shame' is not impossible after assault, but alongside 'defective self' and 'unrecognisable self' it suggests a bodily violation/injury-focused appraisal pattern that is not well reflected in the other selected nodes. The triggers and strategies mainly reflect avoidance, numbing, and offender-related activation rather than body-focused trauma processing.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising others' is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation links Triggers strongly with Maladaptive Strategies and Negative Appraisals strongly with Triggers, but this strategy is not a plausible direct response to the chosen triggers (medical procedures, intrusive thoughts, offender cues) and is not well explained by the selected appraisals. It addresses a generalized harm concern that is otherwise absent from the profile.

vignette:
Gerald is a 70-year-old married man who has worked in retail sales for most of his adult life, a career built on warmth, easy conversation, and the kind of steady confidence that puts customers at ease. He presented for an initial assessment several weeks after being physically assaulted outside a bar he had visited with a former colleague, and the contrast between the man he describes having been and the man who now sits across from the clinician is one of the most striking features of the intake.

The assault occurred on a weeknight in late autumn. Gerald had agreed to meet an acquaintance for a drink after work - something he had done dozens of times over the years without incident. The evening deteriorated when a man at the bar, whom Gerald recognised vaguely from the neighbourhood, became aggressive after a brief, unremarkable exchange. The confrontation moved outside. The man, who smelled strongly of alcohol, struck Gerald repeatedly before bystanders intervened. Gerald sustained bruising to his face and ribs. What stayed with him, however, was not only the physical pain but the particular smell of alcohol on the man's breath in the moments before the first blow landed, the way the man's face looked up close, and the paralysing certainty, in those seconds, that he had somehow invited what was happening by the way he had spoken, by some tone or gesture that had escalated things. He left that night believing, at some level he has never fully articulated until now, that the event had been his own doing.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald found himself unable to pass the block where the bar is located. His sales territory includes that neighbourhood, and he began rerouting his daily calls to avoid it entirely, telling his manager only that he was "trying something different." The detour costs him time and has caused him to miss several accounts he once serviced regularly; one long-standing client has already commented on his absence. At work, where Gerald once moved through the floor with an almost instinctive sociability, he now describes going through the motions - smiling when he knows he is supposed to, but feeling, as he puts it, "like there is glass between me and everyone else." He has come to manage his days by keeping his inner life at a careful distance from the surface, numbing what arises before it can fully form.

At home, he is quieter than his wife has ever known him to be. She has noticed, though he has said little. When unwanted thoughts about the assault surface - the smell, the man's face, the sequence of what he said and what he might have said differently - Gerald pushes against them deliberately, working to crowd them out with tasks or television. The effort is exhausting and rarely complete. What frightens him most in these moments is not the memory itself but what it seems to confirm: that there is something fundamentally wrong with him, some defect in his character that the assault exposed rather than created. He is certain, in a way that resists gentle challenge, that a different man - a better man - would not have found himself in that situation.

The prospect of seeing the man who assaulted him is not abstract. They live in proximity, and Gerald has spotted him twice at a distance since the assault, each time feeling a flood of distress that he has not been able to name cleanly. He has not told his wife about these encounters.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a conversation with his physician during a routine appointment, in which he admitted, almost accidentally, that he had not felt like himself in months. He agreed to a referral with some reluctance. He arrived at the first session describing himself as someone who does not believe in "dwelling," and yet he acknowledged that he no longer recognises the person he has become - the rerouted drives, the glass wall at work, the silence at home. What he hopes for, stated plainly, is to feel like himself again. What he fears, just as plainly, is that the self he is looking for may no longer be available to him.
